title: Autumn Budget 2026: What It Means for Contractors and Sole Traders
description: What the 28 October Budget changed for contractors, sole traders, directors and landlords: worked examples, key dates, and the dividend myth to ignore.
author: Barry Adams
why: The Budget was on 28 October and people are searching for what it means for them now. Written for Focus clients by type of person, and it corrects the dividend-tax mistake other firms are repeating.

html:
Chancellor John Healey delivered the Autumn Budget on Wednesday 28 October 2026.

If you're a contractor, freelancer, sole trader or run a small limited company, the short version is this: most of what you pay day to day hasn't changed. There's no rise in income tax on your salary, no rise in dividend tax, no change to corporation tax, no change to the VAT threshold, and no change to IR35.

What has changed is a handful of things that matter a lot to some people. Those are tax on savings interest and rental income, the limit on Business Asset Disposal Relief, mileage, the trading allowance, and how you'll pay HMRC from 2029.

Rather than walk through every measure, we've grouped what matters by who you are. Skip to the section that fits you.

First, a correction: dividend tax did not go up

We've already seen Budget summaries showing dividend tax rising in April 2027. It isn't.

The 2-point rise in dividend tax was announced in last year's Budget and took effect in April 2026. HMRC's own rates table for this Budget shows dividend rates staying exactly where they are for 2027/28:

Dividend tax 2026/27 (now) 2027/28
Dividend allowance £500 £500
Basic rate 10.75% 10.75%
Higher rate 35.75% 35.75%
Additional rate 39.35% 39.35%

If a summary shows 8.75% and 33.75% as "this year's" rates, it's a year out of date. If you've planned your 2027/28 dividends around it, the numbers are wrong.

If you're a contractor with a limited company

Your salary and dividend mix doesn't need to change because of this Budget. Dividend rates, corporation tax (19% small profits rate, 25% main rate), the £10,500 Employment Allowance and the personal allowance of £12,570 all stay the same. There are no IR35 changes either.

Four things are worth knowing.

1. Buying an electric car through your company? The 100% deadline is 31 March 2027.

A new zero-emission car bought by your company can currently be written off 100% against profits in the year you buy it. That relief ends on 31 March 2027 for companies, and this Budget didn't extend it. What counts is when the car is delivered, so order early. Maria explains the timing, with a £50,000 example, in electric car capital allowances: 100% tax relief ends 31 March 2027.

After that, the car goes into the main pool, and the main writing-down allowance also falls from 14% to 12% from 1 April 2027. Cars are excluded from the new 50% first-year allowance.

£40,000 new electric car bought by your company Delivered by 31 March 2027 Delivered from 1 April 2027
Tax deduction in year one £40,000 £4,800 (12%)
Corporation tax saved in year one (at 25%) £10,000 £1,200

The rest of the relief still comes eventually, but slowly. If an EV through the company was already on your list, the timing now matters. Don't buy a car for the tax break alone. Talk to us first, because benefit-in-kind also rises from 4% to 5% for zero-emission cars in 2027/28.

2. Mileage: the higher rate goes up from April 2027.

If you use your own car for business journeys, the rate for the first 10,000 miles rose to 55p in April 2026, and the Budget has made that permanent. From 6 April 2027 the rate for every mile above 10,000 rises from 25p to 35p.

Here's what that means for someone doing 14,000 business miles a year:

Tax year First 10,000 miles Remaining 4,000 miles Tax-free total
2025/26 £4,500 (45p) £1,000 (25p) £5,500
2026/27 £5,500 (55p) £1,000 (25p) £6,500
2027/28 £5,500 (55p) £1,400 (35p) £6,900

That's £1,400 more a year paid to you tax-free than two years ago, for the same driving. If you're not claiming mileage through your company, or you're logging it loosely, now's the time to fix that. FreeAgent works out mileage claims at the HMRC rates for you, and our guide to HMRC business mileage rates covers what counts as a business journey.

3. The plan to make companies report director's loans and other payments to HMRC has been dropped.

The government consulted earlier this year on making close companies report payments to directors and shareholders, such as director's loans, to HMRC. It has decided not to go ahead with this "at this time". That's one less piece of admin.

4. The rules on taking money out of companies will be updated from April 2028.

The government is pressing ahead with modernising the "distributions" rules, which decide how money taken out of a company is taxed. The current rules date back to 1965. Draft legislation is due in 2027. The government says genuine commercial activity and family succession won't be affected. The detail isn't out yet, so if you're thinking about closing or restructuring your company in 2028 or later, let's look at it together once the draft rules are published.

If you're thinking about closing or selling your company

Business Asset Disposal Relief (BADR) lifetime limit halves to £500,000 from 6 April 2027.

BADR lets you pay 18% Capital Gains Tax instead of 24% on qualifying gains, which includes many contractors closing their company through a members' voluntary liquidation. The rate stays at 18%, but the lifetime amount you can claim it on falls from £1 million to £500,000.

For most contractors, this changes nothing. HMRC expects around 3 in 4 people who claim the relief to be unaffected. It only bites if your lifetime qualifying gains are above £500,000.

If they are, here's the effect on a £700,000 gain (no previous claims, and ignoring the £3,000 annual exemption to keep it simple):

Before 6 April 2027 From 6 April 2027
First £500,000 at 18% £90,000 £90,000
Next £200,000 £36,000 (18%) £48,000 (24%)
Total CGT £126,000 £138,000

That's £12,000 more. The most anyone can lose is £30,000, on gains of £1 million or more.

If you're sitting on large retained profits and were planning to close the company anyway, the timing is worth a conversation now. There are anti-forestalling rules for sales agreed before 6 April 2027 that complete after it, so don't try to rush anything through without advice.

There's also a new Founders' Relief from 6 April 2027: 10% CGT on up to £10 million of gains for founders of fast-growing companies. The qualifying tests are demanding, and they're still out for consultation, so it won't apply to most small companies.

If you're a sole trader or freelancer

New to us? See how we help sole traders and freelancers.

1. The trading allowance triples to £3,000 from 6 April 2027.

Right now, if you earn more than £1,000 a year from self-employment you have to tell HMRC. From 2027/28 that threshold rises to £3,000, both for the tax-free allowance and for the point at which you have to report.

That helps people with a small side income, such as a bit of freelance design work, selling crafts or tutoring a few evenings a month. You can either take the £3,000 allowance or claim your actual expenses, not both. If your costs are higher than £3,000, claiming expenses is still the better route.

2. Making Tax Digital starts on 6 April 2027 for anyone with combined sales and rents received over £30,000.

This was already announced, but it's now five months away. If your combined turnover from self-employment and property was over £30,000 in 2025/26, you'll need to keep digital records and send HMRC quarterly updates from April 2027. Note that it's turnover, not profit.

The Budget added one concession. If you join in April 2027, you won't get late-submission penalty points on your quarterly updates during 2027/28. You'll still have to send all four updates before you can file your tax return, though, so the work doesn't go away.

Our Making Tax Digital guide covers thresholds, deadlines and penalties. Maria runs our MTD review meetings if you'd like to check where you stand.

3. Payments on account will be spread through the year from April 2029.

At the moment, if you pay tax through Self Assessment you probably make two big payments on account, in January and July. From April 2029 the government wants that replaced with smaller, more regular payments during the year, collected automatically. Those with a PAYE job as well may be able to pay through their tax code.

The detail, covering how often you'll pay, what happens if your income drops and what flexibility there'll be, is due next year. HMRC says a tool to estimate your bill and make voluntary payments will arrive in 2028.

This doesn't cost you more tax, but it changes your cashflow. If you currently rely on having the money until January, start thinking about setting some aside monthly. FreeAgent's tax timeline already shows you what you owe as you go, and a FreeAgent subscription is included in all our plans.

4. Self-employed fathers and partners get paid parental leave from April 2029.

For the first time, self-employed fathers, partners and adopters will be able to claim two weeks of paid parental support from April 2029, at up to £194 a week at today's rate.

If you're a landlord or have savings

This is where the Budget bites hardest.

From 6 April 2027, income tax on rental profits (England, Wales and Northern Ireland) and on savings interest (the whole UK) will be charged at:

Now (2026/27) From 6 April 2027
Basic rate 20% 24%
Higher rate 40% 44%
Additional rate 45% 49%

You'll see this reported as a "2% rise". That's 2% on top of the 2% already announced last year, which hasn't started yet. Compared with what you pay today, it's 4 percentage points. That's an extra £40 for every £1,000 of taxable rent or interest.

Landlord example. A basic-rate landlord with £12,000 of rental profit and £4,000 of mortgage interest:

2026/27 2027/28
Tax on £12,000 rental profit £2,400 (20%) £2,880 (24%)
Less mortgage interest credit on £4,000 –£800 (20%) –£960 (24%)
Tax to pay £1,600 £1,920

That's £320 more a year. The mortgage interest credit rises to 24% in line with the new basic property rate. Higher and additional-rate landlords pay 44% or 49% on their profit, but still only get the basic-rate credit on their mortgage interest.

Landlords with companies pay corporation tax on their rental profit, so they aren't affected. That doesn't mean incorporating is right for you, though. Moving an existing portfolio into a company can trigger Capital Gains Tax and Stamp Duty, so it's a decision to take with proper advice. See our landlord accountants page.

Savers. The government says 88% of people will pay no more tax on their savings. The personal savings allowance (£1,000 for basic-rate taxpayers, £500 for higher-rate) is unchanged. The good news is that the planned cut to the cash ISA limit has been dropped, and it stays at £20,000. If you hold significant cash outside an ISA, using your allowance before April 2027 is the simple fix.

If you employ people

  • National Living Wage rises 3.9% to £13.21 an hour from 1 April 2027. The 18–20 rate rises to £11.27 and the 16–17 and apprentice rate to £8.31.
  • The Employment Allowance stays at £10,500.
  • The £2,000 cap on National Insurance-free pension salary sacrifice from April 2029 (announced last year) is going ahead.
  • Company cars, vans and fuel benefits must be payrolled from 6 April 2027, rather than reported on P11Ds.
  • For qualifying retail, hospitality and leisure properties in England, the threshold for 100% small business rates relief rises from £12,000 to £18,000 rateable value from April 2027, with tapered relief up to £21,000.

Changes coming in 2029 that will affect almost everyone

These are a few years off but worth knowing about now:

  • Direct Debit for VAT and PAYE (April 2029). Businesses will have to set up a Direct Debit for VAT and PAYE bills. You can still pay another way before the deadline, and the Direct Debit only collects whatever's left unpaid.
  • HMRC taking smaller debts straight from bank accounts (2029/30). HMRC plans to recover lower-value tax debts through regular deductions from bank accounts where people repeatedly fail to engage. Another reason not to ignore HMRC letters.
  • Mandatory e-invoicing (April 2029). VAT invoices will need to be issued in a set electronic format. Full technical detail is due by April 2028, and we'll make sure your software is ready.

What hasn't changed

It's just as useful to know what you don't need to worry about:

  • Income tax rates on earnings, and the personal allowance of £12,570, are frozen until 2031.
  • Dividend tax rates and the £500 dividend allowance.
  • Corporation tax at 19% and 25%.
  • The VAT registration threshold of £90,000.
  • National Insurance rates and the main thresholds.
  • IR35.
  • The cash ISA limit of £20,000.
  • The Capital Gains Tax rates of 18% and 24%, and the £3,000 annual exemption.

Questions we're being asked

Did dividend tax go up in the 2026 Budget? No. Dividend tax rose in April 2026, following the 2025 Budget. For 2027/28 the rates stay at 10.75%, 35.75% and 39.35%, with a £500 allowance.

When does the new £3,000 trading allowance start? From 6 April 2027, for the 2027/28 tax year. The Self Assessment reporting threshold for trading income also rises to £3,000 at the same time.

Does the BADR change affect contractors closing their company? Only if your lifetime qualifying gains are over £500,000. Below that, you still get the full 18% rate. The new limit applies to disposals on or after 6 April 2027.

What's the mileage rate from April 2027? 55p a mile for the first 10,000 business miles in the tax year, and 35p a mile after that (up from 25p).

Is the property income tax rise 2% or 4%? Compared with what you pay in 2026/27, it's 4 percentage points: 20% to 24%, 40% to 44% and 45% to 49%, from 6 April 2027. The "2%" figure is the extra on top of the rise announced in 2025.

Want to know what it means for you specifically?

Budgets are written for millions of people, but your tax position is yours. If any of the above affects you, or you're not sure whether it does, book a call with Barry, Greg or Maria and we'll work through it with you.

This article reflects the Budget announcements of 28 October 2026. Some measures are subject to consultation and legislation, and the detail may change. It's general information, not personal advice.
